client: I've been having a really hard time since my younger sister passed away six months ago in a car accident. It feels like everything that used to make me happy just feels hollow now, like I'm going through the motions but not actually living. And honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything — like, what can you really say that would make any of this better?
therapist: I'm so deeply sorry for the loss of your sister — that kind of grief can make the whole world feel like it's lost its color, and what you're describing makes complete sense given what you've been through. You're right that no words can undo this pain, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to fix it or say something that makes it all better. I'm wondering, though — when you say you're not sure talking will help, is that coming from a place of exhaustion, like you've maybe already tried to make sense of this and it just hasn't eased anything yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think exhaustion is a big part of it. I've talked to a few people — friends, my mom — and it always ends up feeling like I'm either consoling them about their grief, or they say something like "she's in a better place" and I just want to scream. So I guess I've kind of stopped expecting conversations to actually help, you know?
therapist: What you're describing — ending up as the one holding everyone else's grief, or receiving platitudes that feel completely disconnected from your reality — is such an exhausting and lonely experience, and it makes so much sense that you'd start to protect yourself by lowering your expectations. It takes a particular kind of courage to still show up here even with that guard up. Can you tell me a little more about what a conversation *would* need to feel like for it to actually feel useful to you, even if that's hard to imagine right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I'm not even sure I know what that would look like anymore. I think I just want someone to sit with how awful it is without trying to wrap it up in some kind of lesson or silver lining — like, my sister is gone and that's just terrible, full stop. But even saying that out loud, I wonder if I'm just setting up some impossible standard so that nothing can actually reach me.
therapist: What you just said — that your sister is gone and that's just terrible, full stop — I want you to know I'm not going to add anything to that, because you're absolutely right, and it deserves to just sit there. And I notice there's something really tender in the way you said it, like part of you is bracing even as you speak, almost as if you're not quite sure it's safe to let that be enough. That question you're asking yourself, about whether you're setting an impossible standard — I'm curious, does it feel more like self-protection, or more like a fear that maybe even *you* can't fully let yourself be reached right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me, because I think it might be the second thing — like, I'm scared that if I actually let myself feel the full weight of it, I won't be able to come back from it. There's this part of me that keeps a little distance even from my own grief, like I'm watching it from across the room instead of actually being in it. And I don't know if that's protecting me or just keeping me stuck in this hollow, going-through-the-motions feeling.
therapist: That fear — that feeling the full weight of it means falling into something you can't climb out of — is one of the most common and human responses to profound grief, and it makes complete sense that a part of you has been standing guard to prevent that. What you're describing, watching your grief from across the room, isn't weakness or avoidance; it's your mind doing its best to keep you functional when the alternative feels unsurvivable. I'm curious — when you imagine actually stepping closer to that grief, what do you picture happening, what does that fear tell you it would look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When I imagine it, I picture just completely falling apart — like, ugly crying for days and not being able to go to work or talk to anyone or function at all. And there's also this other fear underneath that one, which is that if I really let myself grieve her fully, it's like I'm accepting that she's actually gone, and some part of me isn't ready to do that yet. I know that probably sounds irrational, but holding back feels like the last bit of control I have over something that was completely out of my control.
therapist: What you just described doesn't sound irrational at all — holding back from grief as a way of holding onto her makes profound sense, because in some way, the grief *is* the goodbye, and you're not ready to say it yet. And that image of falling apart for days, of losing all function — I want to gently offer that grief rarely works quite like that; it tends to come in waves rather than one endless flood, even when we're terrified it won't. I'm wondering, when you imagine "falling apart," is there any part of you that also recognizes that might be your mind's way of making sure you never have to find out whether you could actually survive it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually lands in a way I wasn't expecting — like, yeah, maybe if I never fully go there, I never have to find out if I'm strong enough to survive it, and that way I'm protected from that fear too. But I'm also sitting here thinking, even if that's true, knowing it doesn't automatically make it easier to do anything differently. It's like understanding the lock doesn't mean you suddenly have the key.
therapist: That metaphor is exactly right, and I want to honor it rather than rush past it — insight is a real thing, but it's not the same as healing, and recognizing a pattern doesn't obligate you to immediately dismantle it. I also notice that even as you're saying something quite clear-eyed and almost measured, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds like it's moving fast, like maybe part of you is working hard to stay on top of this rather than inside it. What would it feel like to just slow down for a moment right here — not to do anything differently yet, just to notice what's present?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When I actually try to slow down right now, there's this tightness in my chest that I usually manage to talk around or stay ahead of. It's like as long as I keep analyzing it, I don't have to just feel it sitting there. And slowing down even for this moment feels kind of terrifying, honestly — like I'm standing at the edge of something and I don't know how deep it goes.
therapist: That tightness in your chest — that's not a problem to be solved right now, that's your grief, actually present, asking to be acknowledged. I want you to know that you don't have to jump in or figure out how deep it goes; you can just stand at that edge for a moment and let it be there without it meaning you have to fall. Can you just stay with that tightness for a few seconds, not to change it, just to let it know you've noticed it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I tried, and I just sat with it for a second, and my eyes got kind of watery which I wasn't expecting at all. It's strange because I didn't even do anything — I just let it be there — and it felt both smaller and bigger at the same time, like it was real in a way I'd been keeping it from being. I don't really know what to do with that.
therapist: What just happened in that moment is actually significant — you didn't analyze your way through it or stay ahead of it, you just let it exist, and it met you back. That feeling of it being both smaller and bigger at once makes complete sense, because when grief is finally allowed to be real, it loses some of its terrifying unknowable quality even as it becomes more present. You don't have to do anything with it right now — what you just did *was* something.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I needed to hear that what I did was something, because my first instinct was to immediately dismiss it as "just tearing up a little" and not a big deal. But sitting here now, I feel kind of raw and exposed in a way I haven't in a while, and I'm not sure if that's good or just uncomfortable. I guess I'm a little scared that this feeling will just close back up the moment I leave here and I'll go back to watching from across the room again.
therapist: That instinct to immediately minimize — "just tearing up a little" — is worth noticing, because it's the same part of you that's been keeping the grief at arm's length, and it moved fast. The rawness you're feeling right now is real, and it makes sense that there's fear wrapped around it, because openness can feel like exposure when you've been protected for a long time. What if, instead of trying to hold onto this feeling or prevent it from closing back up, you just let yourself remember that you found your way here once — which means some part of you knows how to find it again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a gentler way of thinking about it than I expected, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But I also notice I'm already a little skeptical, like — what if the reason I found my way here was because this is a structured, safe environment, and real life just doesn't have that same container around it? I guess I'm worried that outside of this room, the grief just becomes something I'm drowning in alone again rather than something I can actually be with.
therapist: That fear of losing the container is real and worth taking seriously, not dismissing — and it actually tells me something important, that part of you *wants* to be able to carry this differently, which is different from not caring. What you found today wasn't created by this room; the room just made it quieter enough for you to hear something that was already in you. I'm wondering if we could think together about what small things in your daily life might offer even a fraction of that quiet — not to replace this, but so you're not starting from zero each time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
